text: And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth…
reflection: Moses had asked to see God's glory. God placed him in a cleft of the rock, covered him with His hand, and passed by. And as He passed, He proclaimed His own name: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." This is how God chose to describe Himself. Not first as powerful, though He is. Not first as holy, though He is. But as merciful, gracious, patient, and full of goodness and truth. These words were spoken right after Israel had worshipped the golden calf. They had broken the covenant almost as soon as they made it. And God responded by revealing His mercy. This description is repeated throughout the Old Testament. Psalms, prophets, and prayers return to it again and again. It became Israel's confession of who God is. This month we will reflect on the character of God. Begin with His own words about Himself. He is merciful and gracious. Rest in that today.
question: Which of God's own words about Himself, merciful, gracious, longsuffering, or abundant in goodness, do you most need today?
prayer: Lord, You are merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth. Thank You for describing Yourself this way, even to people who had failed You. I rest in who You are. Amen.

text: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
reflection: At the burning bush, God called Moses to go to Pharaoh and lead Israel out of Egypt. Moses asked a reasonable question: when the people ask who sent me, what shall I tell them? God answered, "I AM THAT I AM." And He added, "Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you." This name is unlike any other. It speaks of God's self-existence. He simply is. He depends on nothing and no one. He was not created. He does not change. He is the source of all existence, and His being has no beginning and no end. Everything else in the universe depends on something else. Only God simply is. This was exactly what Moses needed. He was facing the most powerful king on earth. But he was sent by the One who is. Whatever you face today, you are not dealing with a God who might be or used to be. He is. Lean on the great I AM.
question: What are you facing today that you could lean on the great I AM for?
prayer: Lord, You are I AM THAT I AM. You depend on nothing, and You have no beginning or end. Whatever I face today, I lean on You. Amen.

text: For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
reflection: Malachi spoke to a people who had grown careless with God. They questioned His love, cheated in their offerings, and broke faith with one another. They deserved judgment. Yet God said, "For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed." Their survival depended on God's unchanging nature. If God were fickle, if His promises could be withdrawn on a whim, they would have been destroyed. But God had made a covenant with Jacob's descendants, and He does not change His mind. His faithfulness held even when theirs failed. This is wonderful news. People change. Moods change. Circumstances change. Even our own commitment to God rises and falls. But God's character remains constant. His love does not cool. His promises do not expire. His mercy does not run out. You can build your life on a God who does not change. On your worst day, He is the same as on your best. Rest in His constancy today.
question: When your own faithfulness wavers, how does God's unchanging nature give you hope?
prayer: Lord, You do not change, and that is why I am not consumed. Thank You that my hope rests on Your faithfulness, not mine. Amen.

text: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
reflection: Balak, king of Moab, hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. But every time Balaam opened his mouth, God turned the curse into a blessing. Frustrated, Balak kept trying different locations, hoping God would change His mind. Balaam finally explained why it would not work: "God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?" People lie. People change their minds. People make promises they do not keep. But God is not like us. When He says something, He means it. When He makes a promise, He fulfils it. He does not need to repent, or change course, because He never makes mistakes. This means every promise in Scripture is completely reliable. If God has said it, He will do it. When you doubt whether God will come through, remember this verse. He has spoken, and He will make it good.
question: Which promise of God do you need to trust He will keep today?
prayer: Lord, You are not a man that You should lie. What You have spoken, You will do. Help me trust Your promises today, every one of them. Amen.

text: He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.
reflection: Near the end of his life, Moses taught Israel a song. It celebrated God's faithfulness and warned against turning away. One of its central lines describes God like this: "He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he." A rock was a powerful image in the wilderness. It meant stability in shifting sands, shade in the heat, protection from enemies, and even water, as when God brought water from the rock. God is all of these. He is unshakable. And Moses adds more. His work is perfect. Nothing He does is flawed. All His ways are just. He is a God of truth, without any wrongdoing. Just and right is He. In a world where leaders fail and systems are unjust, there is One who is completely right. You can rest your full weight on Him. He will not crumble or shift. He is the Rock.
question: What are you leaning on that is shifting, and how could you rest your full weight on the Rock?
prayer: Lord, You are the Rock; Your work is perfect, and all Your ways are just and true. In a shifting world, I rest my full weight on You today. Amen.

text: And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
reflection: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw a vision of the Lord seated on a high throne. The train of His robe filled the temple. Above Him stood seraphim, heavenly beings who covered their faces and feet, and cried to one another, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Holiness is repeated three times. In Hebrew, repetition was a way of emphasizing. To say holy three times is to say God is supremely, utterly, infinitely holy. He is set apart from everything else, perfect in purity and goodness. Isaiah's response was immediate: Woe is me! I am undone. He saw his own sinfulness in the light of God's holiness. But God sent a seraph with a live coal to touch his lips and take away his sin. Encountering God's holiness humbles us, but it also leads to cleansing. Reflect on His holiness today. Let it humble you, and let His grace cleanse you.
question: How does seeing God's holiness change the way you see yourself and His grace?
prayer: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts. Like Isaiah, I see my own need before You. Thank You for Your cleansing grace that takes my sin away. Amen.

text: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.
reflection: God's people in exile felt forgotten. They complained that God did not see their troubles. Isaiah answered with a series of questions: "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?" Everyone gets tired. The strongest people need rest. Even the most dedicated workers burn out. But God never does. He does not faint. He does not grow weary. He never needs a break from caring for you. He never sleeps on the job. His energy and attention are limitless. And the verse adds, "there is no searching of his understanding." His wisdom is beyond our comprehension. He understands what we cannot. When you feel unseen, remember that God is never too tired to notice you. When you feel confused, remember that His understanding has no limit. Isaiah goes on to say that this tireless God gives power to the faint. His strength is available to you.
question: Where are you weary, and how does it help to know that God never faints or grows tired?
prayer: Everlasting God, You never faint and never grow weary, and Your understanding is beyond searching. When I run out of strength, let me rest in Yours. Amen.

text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD.
reflection: Isaiah 55 is an invitation to come to God, to seek Him while He may be found, and to return to Him so He can have mercy. In the middle of it, God explains why His mercy is so surprising: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD." In context, this is about God's willingness to forgive. Human beings hold grudges. We keep score. We find it hard to forgive great wrongs. But God thinks differently. His mercy goes far beyond ours. Where we would give up on someone, He extends pardon. This verse is also a reminder of humility. We cannot fully understand God. His thoughts are not like ours. When He acts in ways we do not expect, it is not because He is wrong but because He sees more. We are not the measure of what God should do. If you are struggling to understand His ways right now, let this verse remind you. His thoughts are different. Trust Him anyway.
question: Where have God's ways surprised you, and how could you trust Him there?
prayer: Lord, Your thoughts are not my thoughts, and Your ways are not my ways. Thank You for Your abundant willingness to forgive. Help me trust You when You surprise me. Amen.

text: For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
reflection: God continues His explanation: "For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts." Look up at the night sky and try to measure the distance to the stars. It is beyond comprehension. That, God says, is the gap between His ways and ours. This is not meant to make God seem distant or cold. In context, it is about the vastness of His mercy and the certainty of His plans. The very next verses compare His word to rain and snow that water the earth and make it fruitful. His word does not return empty. It accomplishes what He sends it to do. So the height of His ways is good news. His plans are bigger than our plans. His wisdom is deeper than our wisdom. His mercy is wider than our mercy. If your own understanding has reached its limit, look up. Remember how high the heavens are. His ways are higher still.
question: What situation could you look up from today and trust to God's higher ways?
prayer: Lord, as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are Your ways higher than mine. Thank You that Your mercy and plans are greater than I can imagine. I trust You today. Amen.

text: Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee…
reflection: Jeremiah was in prison, and Jerusalem was surrounded by the Babylonian army. The city was about to fall. And God told Jeremiah to buy a field. It seemed absurd. Who buys land in a country about to be conquered? But Jeremiah obeyed, and then he prayed: "Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee." The purchase was a sign that God would one day restore His people to the land. Jeremiah could not see how. But he started his prayer with God's power in creation. If God made the heavens and the earth, then nothing is too hard for Him. Not a besieged city. Not a hopeless situation. Not a broken life. What feels impossible to you today? A relationship, a health problem, a financial need, a habit you cannot break? Bring it to the God who made heaven and earth. Nothing is too hard for Him.
question: What impossible situation could you bring to the God who made heaven and earth today?
prayer: Ah Lord GOD, You made the heaven and the earth by Your great power, and there is nothing too hard for You. I bring You my impossible situation today. Amen.

text: The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.
reflection: Jeremiah 31 is a chapter of hope, written to a people facing exile. In it, God speaks these tender words: "Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee." Everlasting love. It did not begin when Israel became faithful, and it would not end when they failed. It stretches from eternity past to eternity future. And because of that love, God draws His people to Himself. He does not wait for us to find our way back. He pulls us close with lovingkindness. Many people struggle to believe God loves them. They know about His love in theory, but they feel unworthy, forgotten, or rejected. This verse speaks directly to that. His love is not based on your performance. It is everlasting. It was there before you were born, and it will remain forever. And He is drawing you toward Himself even now. Let these words sink deep into your heart today. You are loved with an everlasting love.
question: Where do you still feel you must earn God's love, and how does His everlasting love answer that?
prayer: Lord, You have loved me with an everlasting love, and with lovingkindness You have drawn me. Let this truth sink deep into my heart today. Amen.

text: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
reflection: David asks two questions in Psalm 139: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" Then he answers them. If I go up to heaven, You are there. If I make my bed in the grave, You are there. If I take the wings of the morning and settle at the far end of the sea, even there Your hand will lead me. There is nowhere beyond God's presence. This can be uncomfortable if we are trying to hide from Him. Jonah tried to run from God and found Him in the belly of a fish. But for those who belong to God, His presence everywhere is a great comfort. You cannot wander so far that He cannot reach you. You cannot fall so low that He is not there. Hospital rooms, lonely apartments, foreign countries, and dark nights are all within His reach. Wherever you are today, God is there. You are never out of His sight or beyond His care.
question: Wherever you go today, how could you remember that God is there?
prayer: Lord, there is nowhere I can go from Your presence. Wherever I am today, You are there. Thank You for the comfort of Your nearness. Amen.

text: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
reflection: After reflecting on God's presence everywhere, David turns to how God formed him in his mother's womb. And he bursts into praise: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well." Fearfully means with awe and reverence. Wonderfully means distinctly, set apart. David marvels at the intricate design of the human body and soul. He sees himself as one of God's marvellous works. Many people struggle to see themselves this way. They focus on their flaws, compare themselves to others, or believe they have little worth. But this verse declares that every person is a careful, intentional work of God. Your existence is not an accident. You were designed with care by a loving Creator. This truth should shape how we see ourselves and others. Every person we meet is fearfully and wonderfully made. Thank God today for how He made you. Then treat others as His marvellous works too.
question: What could you thank God for about the way He made you, and how could you see others as His work too?
prayer: Lord, I will praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Thank You for the care You took in making me, and help me see others as Your marvellous works too. Amen.

text: He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.
reflection: Look up on a clear night far from city lights, and you will see thousands of stars. Astronomers estimate there are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all the beaches of the earth. Yet Psalm 147 says, "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names." God knows exactly how many there are. And He knows each one by name. This shows the vastness of His power and knowledge. Nothing in creation is too big for Him to manage or too small for Him to notice. But this verse is not just about astronomy. Look at the verse before it: He heals the broken in heart. The God who names the stars is the same God who binds up wounded hearts. His greatness does not make Him distant. It makes Him able to care for each of us personally. If He knows every star by name, He certainly knows yours. No one is lost in the crowd to Him. He sees you.
question: If God knows every star by name, how does it change things to know He knows yours?
prayer: Lord, You count the stars and call them all by name. You are vast in power, yet You know me personally. Thank You that I am never lost to You. Amen.

text: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
reflection: Psalm 147 was likely written after the exiles returned to Jerusalem. The people had been scattered, wounded, and grieving. The psalm celebrates God gathering them back. And in the middle of it is this tender verse: "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds." A broken heart is one of the deepest pains a person can experience. Grief, betrayal, rejection, and loss can shatter us inside. And often, no one else can see the wound. But God sees it. And He heals it. The image of binding up wounds is gentle and personal. It is the work of someone who kneels beside the injured, cleans the wound, and wraps it with care. That is how God treats the brokenhearted. He does not rush past pain or demand that we get over it. He tends to it patiently. If your heart is broken today, bring it to Him. Let Him bind up your wounds. He is a gentle healer.
question: What broken place in your heart could you bring to God for healing today?
prayer: Lord, You heal the broken in heart and bind up their wounds. You see the pain I hide. I bring my broken heart to You and ask for Your patient, healing care. Amen.

text: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him.
reflection: How does God feel about you when you struggle or fail? Psalm 103 answers with a picture from family life: "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him." Pitieth means shows compassion. A good father does not look at his struggling child with contempt. He looks with tenderness. When a small child falls, a loving father picks them up. When a child is frightened, he comforts them. When a child fails, he does not reject them. That is how God looks at those who fear Him. And the next verse explains why: "For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust." God knows our limitations. He knows how weak and frail we are. He does not expect us to be stronger than we are. His compassion is shaped by His understanding of our weakness. Some people had harsh or absent fathers, and this image is hard for them. But God is the Father we always needed. Let Him show you His compassion today.
question: Where do you need God's fatherly compassion for your weakness today?
prayer: Father, as a father pities his children, so You pity those who fear You. You know my frame and remember that I am dust. Show me Your compassion today. Amen.

text: Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
reflection: Moses, who wrote Psalm 90, had seen a lot of change. He had grown up in Pharaoh's palace, fled to the desert, led a nation, and watched a generation die in the wilderness. Against the backdrop of all that change, he wrote, "Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God." Mountains seem ancient and permanent to us. But before there were mountains, God was. Before the earth existed, God was. From everlasting in the past to everlasting in the future, He is God. Our lives are short. Moses goes on to compare them to grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening. But God is eternal. This truth puts our worries in perspective. The God who existed before the mountains is not threatened by today's problems. And it gives us security. Our short lives are held by an eternal God. Rest today in the One who is from everlasting to everlasting.
question: How does knowing your short life is held by an eternal God bring you peace today?
prayer: Lord, from everlasting to everlasting, You are God. My life is short, but it is held in Your eternal hands. I rest today in the One who was before all things. Amen.

text: The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations.
reflection: Psalm 33 contrasts human plans with God's plans. Nations make plans, and God brings them to nothing. Rulers devise schemes, and God overturns them. But then the psalmist says, "The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations." Human plans come and go. Empires rise and fall. Ideologies sweep through cultures and then fade. Even our personal plans often fall apart. But God's counsel, His purposes and decisions, stand forever. Nothing can overturn them. They continue from generation to generation. This is a stabilizing truth. When the news is full of turmoil, God's plans are not threatened. When your own plans collapse, His purposes for you remain. He is working out something that will last. And the phrase the thoughts of his heart reminds us that His plans are not cold calculations. They come from His heart. They are shaped by His love. Trust His plans today. They will stand.
question: What plan of yours has fallen apart, and how could you trust God's plans instead?
prayer: Lord, Your counsel stands for ever, and the thoughts of Your heart to all generations. When my plans fall apart, help me trust Yours. Amen.

text: And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?
reflection: Hagar was a servant girl in Abraham's household. She had been mistreated by Sarah and fled into the wilderness, pregnant and alone. She had no one. No status, no protector, no future. By a spring in the desert, the angel of the Lord found her. He spoke to her, gave her a promise, and told her to return. Hagar was amazed. "And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me." Hagar is the only person in the Bible who gave God a name. And the name she chose was the God who sees. In a world where she was invisible, God saw her. He noticed her pain. He knew her name. He cared about her future and her child's future. If you feel invisible today, unnoticed by others, overlooked or forgotten, remember Hagar. The God who found her in the wilderness sees you too. You are not hidden from Him. He is the God who sees.
question: Where do you feel unseen right now, and how does it help to know God sees you?
prayer: Lord, You are the God who sees. When I feel invisible or overlooked, remind me that You see me and know exactly where I am. Amen.

text: And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovah-jireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen.
reflection: God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac, the son of promise, on Mount Moriah. Abraham obeyed, trusting God. As they climbed, Isaac asked where the lamb for the offering was. Abraham answered that God would provide Himself a lamb. At the last moment, an angel stopped him, and Abraham saw a ram caught in a thicket. He offered it in place of his son. "And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovah-jireh." The name means the Lord will provide, or the Lord will see to it. Abraham did not know how God would provide. But he trusted that He would. And God did, in a way Abraham could not have planned. This place became a memorial of God's provision. Centuries later, on these same hills, God would provide the ultimate Lamb in His own Son. Whatever you need today, God sees it. He will provide, perhaps in ways you cannot yet imagine. Trust Jehovah-jireh.
question: What need could you trust the Lord to provide for in a way you cannot plan?
prayer: Lord, You are Jehovah-jireh, the Lord who provides. You see my needs before I do. Help me trust You to provide in ways I cannot plan. Amen.

text: And said, If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee.
reflection: Just after crossing the Red Sea, Israel came to a place called Marah, where the water was bitter. The people grumbled. Moses cried out to God, who showed him a tree. When Moses threw it into the water, the water became sweet. Then God made a promise and revealed another of His names: "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." God is a healer. He heals bodies, but He also heals hearts, relationships, and broken lives. At Marah, He turned bitter water sweet. He can do the same with bitter places in our lives. The promise was connected to listening and obeying. God's ways are not arbitrary. They are healthy. Walking in them protects us from much harm. But even when we fail, God remains the Healer. Not every illness is healed in this life, and we may not understand why. But God's nature as Healer never changes. Bring your bitter waters to Him today. Ask Him to heal what is broken.
question: What bitter place in your life could you bring to the Lord who heals?
prayer: Lord, You made the bitter waters sweet and revealed Yourself as the Lord who heals. I bring You my bitter places today. Heal me in body, heart, and life. Amen.

text: Then Gideon built an altar there unto the LORD, and called it Jehovah-shalom: unto this day it is yet in Ophrah of the Abi-ezrites.
reflection: Gideon was hiding. The Midianites had been raiding Israel for years, and Gideon was secretly threshing wheat in a winepress so they would not find it. Then the angel of the Lord appeared and called him a mighty man of valour. Gideon was terrified, especially when he realized he had seen the angel of the Lord face to face. He thought he would die. But God said, Peace be unto thee; fear not. In response, "Gideon built an altar there unto the LORD, and called it Jehovah-shalom." The Lord is peace. Shalom is more than the absence of conflict. It means wholeness, completeness, and well-being. God is not only the giver of peace. He is peace. When we have Him, we have the source of true wholeness. Gideon was afraid, weak, and unsure of himself. Yet God met him with peace. If fear has you hiding today, listen for God's word to Gideon. Peace be unto thee. Fear not. The Lord is your peace.
question: Where is fear keeping you hidden, and how could you receive God's peace there today?
prayer: Lord, You are Jehovah-shalom, the Lord who is peace. When fear has me hiding, speak peace to me as You did to Gideon. Amen.

text: He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
reflection: John's first letter contains one of the shortest and most profound statements in the Bible: "for God is love." Not just that God loves, though He does. But that love is His very nature. Love is not something God does occasionally. It is who He is. Everything He does flows from love: creating, providing, disciplining, forgiving, and saving. John places this truth next to a challenge: "He that loveth not knoweth not God." If God is love, then knowing Him will make us loving. People who claim to know God but have no love for others reveal that they do not really know Him. This does not mean we love perfectly. But it means love should be growing in us, because God's nature is rubbing off on us as we walk with Him. Today, let this simple truth sink in. God is love. His love for you is not a mood that might change. It is His nature. And let His love flow through you to others.
question: How could God's love flow through you to someone today?
prayer: Lord, You are love. Let that truth sink deep into my heart, and let Your love flow through me to the people I meet today. Amen.

text: This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
reflection: John also wrote, "This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." Light is a picture of purity, truth, and goodness. Darkness pictures sin, deception, and evil. God is entirely light. There is no shadow in Him. No hidden agenda, no mixed motives. He is completely good and completely true. This matters because we are surrounded by mixed things. People we admire have flaws. Leaders we trust can fail us. Even our own hearts are a mix of good and bad. But God is pure light. We never have to wonder whether He is secretly against us or hiding something. He is wholly good. This also means walking with Him involves walking in the light. We cannot hold on to darkness and enjoy fellowship with Him at the same time. Today, thank God that He is pure light. Then step into that light, and let it shine on every part of your life.
question: What part of your life could you bring into God's light today?
prayer: Lord, You are light, and in You is no darkness at all. Thank You for Your perfect goodness. Help me step into Your light and walk there today. Amen.

text: There is none holy as the LORD: for there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God.
reflection: Hannah had prayed for years for a child. When God finally gave her Samuel, she dedicated him to the Lord. And then she prayed a song of praise. It begins with joy and soon turns to God's character: "There is none holy as the LORD: for there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God." Hannah had been mocked and humiliated by Peninnah, her rival. But Hannah's song is not about getting even. It is about God. She realized that He is incomparable. No one is holy like Him. No one else is God. No one is a rock like Him. When we have walked through pain and seen God answer, we often see Him more clearly. Our trials reveal His character in ways comfort never could. Her song goes on to praise God for lifting the humble and raising the poor from the dust. Today, join Hannah. Praise God for who He is. There is none like Him.
question: How has a trial shown you something about God that comfort never could?
prayer: Lord, there is none holy like You, and there is no rock like our God. Thank You for showing Yourself through every trial and every answer. I praise You for who You are. Amen.

text: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
reflection: Job had asked God many questions in his suffering. Why was this happening? Where was God? Finally, God answered out of a whirlwind. But instead of giving explanations, He asked questions of His own: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Then God took Job on a tour of creation. The oceans, the stars, the storehouses of snow, the wild animals, the eagle in flight. Each question revealed God's vast wisdom and power, and Job's limited understanding. This was not God being harsh. It was God showing Job who He is. Job's response was humility and worship. He said he had heard of God before, but now he saw Him. Job never received a full explanation for his suffering. But he received something better: a fresh vision of God. Sometimes we want answers, but what we need is God Himself. Look at His creation today. Let it show you His greatness, and let that be enough.
question: What in creation could you look at today to remind you of God's greatness?
prayer: Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth. When I do not have all the answers, let a fresh vision of Your greatness be enough for me today. Amen.

text: For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
reflection: Paul spent three chapters of Romans wrestling with the mysteries of God's plan. Then he burst into praise, ending with this: "For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen." Of him: God is the source of everything. Nothing exists that did not come from Him. Through him: God sustains everything. Nothing continues apart from His power. To him: God is the goal of everything. All things exist for His glory. This one verse covers the beginning, middle, and end of all creation. Everything starts with God, is held together by God, and returns to God. That includes your life. You came from Him. You are held by Him. And your life finds its purpose in Him. When we see things this way, our perspective shifts. Life is not about us. It is about Him. And that is freeing, not diminishing. We are part of something far bigger than ourselves. To Him be glory for ever.
question: How would it reshape your day to see that all things are of God, through God, and to God?
prayer: Lord, of You, and through You, and to You are all things. My life begins, continues, and finds its purpose in You. To You be glory for ever. Amen.

text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
reflection: James warned his readers not to blame God for temptation. God does not tempt anyone to sin. Instead, He is the source of everything good: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning." The Father of lights is a reference to God as Creator of the sun, moon, and stars. Those lights shift. The sun rises and sets. The moon waxes and wanes. Shadows move throughout the day. But God does not shift. He has no variableness. He does not cast changing shadows. His goodness is constant. Every good thing in your life comes from Him. The warmth of friendship, the beauty of a sunset, the taste of good food, the joy of laughter, and the gift of salvation. All of it flows down from the Father of lights. Today, trace the good things in your life back to their source. Thank the unchanging Giver for each one.
question: What good things in your life could you trace back to the Father of lights today?
prayer: Father of lights, every good and perfect gift comes from You, and You never change. Help me trace the good in my life back to You and thank You for it today. Amen.

text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
reflection: The book of Hebrews was written to believers tempted to drift back to old ways. Their leaders had passed away, their circumstances were difficult, and they needed something solid to hold on to. In the middle of the final chapter is this short declaration: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever." Leaders change. Teachers come and go. Circumstances shift. But Jesus does not change. The Jesus who healed the sick, welcomed sinners, calmed storms, and forgave His enemies is the same Jesus today. His love has not cooled. His power has not weakened. His promises have not expired. And He will be the same forever. This is why we can trust Him completely. We do not have to wonder whether He will still be merciful tomorrow, or whether His grace will still be enough next year. He is the same. When everything else in your life feels uncertain, hold on to this. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
question: What feels uncertain right now that you could hold up against the unchanging Christ?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. When everything else shifts, I hold on to You. Your love and promises never change. Amen.

text: The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.
reflection: Psalm 145 is a song of praise from David, celebrating God's greatness and goodness. In the middle of it is this simple, sweeping statement: "The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works." Good to all. Not just to the deserving. Not just to those who believe. God sends rain on the just and the unjust. He gives breath to every person. He feeds the birds and clothes the fields with flowers. His goodness touches every part of creation. And His tender mercies are over all His works. Like a mother bird spreading her wings over her nest, God's compassion covers everything He has made. This month we have reflected on the character of God. He is merciful, unchanging, holy, faithful, loving, all-seeing, and good. We have only touched the edges of who He is. But this final truth sums it up well. The Lord is good. Not just sometimes, but always. Not just to some, but to all. Thank Him today.
question: Where have you seen God's goodness to all this month, and how could you thank Him for it?
prayer: Lord, You are good to all, and Your tender mercies are over all Your works. As this month ends, I thank You for Your goodness to me and to all You have made. Amen.
